item.title: Young Cinephiles
item.description:
Good morning! Have you been seeing a lot of movies lately? Me too. Let’s talk about it.

There’s been a notable rise of Gen Z cinephiles. My colleague found that our generation has been flocking to theaters to see indies, classics and blockbusters. Social isolation and social media may have something to do with it.

Recently, I’ve seen “Primetime,” “You Can See Everything” and “Club Kid.” “La Bola Negra” and “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” are next on my list.

What movies are you excited about? Email me.

We’re also covering:

A global outage

Bonobos

Sweet treats

What to discuss in class today.

1. Senator Chris Van Hollen said he would challenge Senator Chuck Schumer for majority leader. The announcement set up a clash among Democrats.

2. Microsoft is trying to fix a global outage. The company is working to improve services for the hundreds of millions of people affected.

3. President Trump urged Jensen Huang to fight for his job before he resigned. The president continued to support the Nvidia chief even as the spy scandal was intensifying. We traced Huang’s downfall.

4. Paul LePage, a Republican, flipped a House seat in Maine. The former governor defeated his progressive challenger.

5. Trump pulled Vice President JD Vance off Iran peace talks. The president said that Vance’s time would be better spent investigating fraud in Democratic-run jurisdictions.

6. Rescue efforts in the Brooklyn building collapse have ended. At least eight people died in the sudden collapse, which turned a busy neighborhood into a disaster zone.

Here’s what Cat Amy, 21, a communication studies major at the University of Georgia, does outside class.

What’s your side hustle? I help build and paint sets for my university theater, as well as helping to make or source props.

Pay: $11 an hour.

Hours per week: Currently four, but I’ve worked up to eight.

How’d you get the gig? I volunteered to work on a university musical during my freshman year, and our technical director asked if I’d like to work in the scene shop for pay.

Why do you like it? It fulfills my creative impulses and has taught me a lot about carpentry, art and production. However, I have to dress to anticipate sawdust, paint and manual labor. Bye bye, cute class outfits :(

Students at Tougaloo College and other nearby historically Black institutions in Mississippi danced and wept over the victory of Scott Colom, who will be the state’s first Black senator since the Reconstruction era.

Protesters in Ireland threw projectiles and what appeared to be milk at former President Joe Biden after he attended an event at Trinity College Dublin.

It’s time for Week 11 of college football. Some of the big games: Wake Forest at S.M.U., Duke at Miami and U.S.C. at Indiana. Here are The Athletic’s predictions.

Students and workers at Starbucks held rallies at more than 40 college campuses across the country to support the Starbucks Workers United boycott campaign, according to The Guardian. Read coverage about the rallies in The Daily Pennsylvanian and The Daily Northwestern.

The University of Chicago removed a definition of gender from its website after pushback from a conservative student publication. (The Chicago Maroon)

The stories about to hit your group chat

The S.S. United States has sunk to the ocean floor. Don’t worry, it’s on purpose. The 20th-century ocean liner will be repurposed into an artificial reef.

Bonobos are challenging our understanding of early human societies. New research found that female bonobos are vicious hunters, challenging the “man the hunter” origin story.

Do this to get ahead.

Bake a sweet treat. I know I can’t stop talking about Thanksgiving, but I can’t help it. I’m planning to make a corn pudding, and I may try to make a dessert this year. These are the best ones.

Travel smart. Heading home for the holidays? Read these 44 essential travel tips from our friends at Wirecutter.

Did you keep up with the headlines this week? Take our news quiz.

Thanks for hanging out with me this morning. This newsletter is powered by your submissions — tell us about your classes, questions, crushes, side hustles and obsessions here.

Also: Times access is free for half of all U.S. college students through their school. Tell your friends to check if their school provides free access.

And forward this to your roommate, professor, club president or T.A. See you next week!

Want more of today’s top stories? Tune in to “The Headlines,” our podcast that includes top headlines and analysis.

Any tips or feedback? I’m all ears. Email me at extracredit@nytimes.com.

The editor of Extra Credit is Talya Minsberg. Harrison Hill and Scott Ball were our photo editors.

item.title: New York to Review School Hiring After Aide Arrested in Jogger Killing
item.description:
The New York City Department of Education said on Friday that it had requested an independent review of its hiring and vetting procedures after a school employee with a history of erratic behavior was charged with fatally stabbing a Brooklyn jogger.

Kamar Samuels, the chancellor of the city’s school system, the largest in the United States, said he had asked the city’s Law Department to lead the investigation, which would include an examination of how information about job applicants is shared among city agencies.

The move was prompted by the arrest this month of Sayed Mohassib, 27, a paraprofessional at a Brooklyn elementary school who was charged in the stabbing death of the jogger, Katie Suarez. Mr. Mohassib has not yet entered a plea in the case.

Mr. Mohassib worked one on one with students with disabilities at Public School 200, located about a mile from where Mr. Suarez, 28, was stabbed along the waterfront in southern Brooklyn on Oct. 30.

He had been hired despite apparent warning signs in his employment history — including a short stint at the Police Department that ended when he was denied reinstatement and an abrupt discharge from the Marine Corps — as well as several mental health episodes, according to police officials and a military spokesman.

“The safety of our students and staff is our highest priority,” Mr. Samuels said in a statement. “We stand ready to immediately take action based on their recommendations.”

The arrest of Mr. Mohassib has stunned parents and colleagues at P.S. 200, also known as the Benson School, who have questioned how he could have passed a department background check and been hired to work closely with students. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said this week that the city would review his hiring.

A colleague at the elementary school said that Mr. Mohassib had shared details with co-workers about his mental health struggles, including an episode that occurred at home while he was working at a high school that resulted in him being hospitalized for three months. The colleague, Natale Di Maggio, said that Mr. Mohassib had claimed to have stopped taking his medication for mental health issues.

“He said he didn’t need them,” said Mr. Di Maggio, a paraprofessional.

Mr. Mohassib started at P.S. 200 last school year, Mr. Di Maggio said. When he arrived for the new school year in September, he looked noticeably different, Mr. Di Maggio said. He had lost a lot of weight and swapped the slacks he had once worn for baggy pants.

Some co-workers felt uncomfortable around Mr. Mohassib and kept their distance, according to two other people familiar with the concerns.

They said Mr. Mohassib had asked teachers to follow him on Instagram, where he had posted shirtless photos of his large tattoos — a shark and a tiger on his chest and cascading words on his stomach that included “Donald J. Trump,” “the Antichrist” and “death.”

Mr. Mohassib first joined the Department of Education in 2019 as a full-time school aide, according to city payroll records. To be hired, he would have had to be nominated by a principal, complete a questionnaire that includes questions about job terminations and military service, and pass a background check, which involves a review of past employment and any criminal history.

He later left the department and entered the Police Academy in April 2022. Mr. Mohassib started working as a police officer that October but was granted military leave near the end of November. About two weeks later, he was discharged.

“The character of his service was incongruent with the Marine Corps’ expectations and standards,” Capt. Jacob M. Sugg, a military spokesman, said.

In January 2023, Mr. Mohassib tried to rejoin the Police Department, police officials said. But when he met with department supervisors, they became so concerned about his behavior and his disheveled appearance that he was taken to Bellevue Hospital, the officials said.

But he was soon able to rejoin the Education Department. Despite his previous employment, his rehiring would have required another nomination, another questionnaire and another background check, according to two people with knowledge of Mr. Mohassib’s hiring.

Whether the department asked about his string of brief jobs or whether he disclosed his mental health history remains unclear.

Chelsia Rose Marcius contributed reporting. Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

item.title: Bloomberg Will Seed a New Pro-Charter School Group With $1 Million
item.description:
A new group has entered the battle over charter schools in New York, seeded with at least $1 million from Michael R. Bloomberg, according to four people familiar with his political spending.

The group, Great Public Schools New York, was formed this week and will be led by Kevin Elkins, a former political director for the carpenters union based in New York City and an adviser to former Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo during his failed mayoral campaign last year.

The group will immediately work to lift the state’s cap on charter schools and to create funding parity with traditional public schools, Mr. Elkins said, and it will not “be shy about building a war chest and using it.”

He said that the group planned to “constructively engage” with Mayor Zohran Mamdani, an ardent supporter of traditional public schools and the teachers’ union. The union vehemently opposes charter schools, which are largely non-unionized. Mr. Elkins said that the mayor’s focus on affordability aligned with the new organization’s push for more choice in education.

“The mayor has changed his positions on several matters since he’s come into City Hall, not because he’s giving up on his ideological convictions, but because he understands that governing is a complicated task,” Mr. Elkins said in an interview.

Dora Pekec, a spokeswoman for Mr. Mamdani, declined to comment on the group, which has an affiliated 501(c)(4), or nonprofit “social welfare organization,” that can engage in political activity and is sometimes called a dark-money group.

Mr. Bloomberg — a former mayor of New York City, a billionaire philanthropist and a political donor — already funds several other prominent and well-endowed organizations that back the expansion of charter schools in the city. A person familiar with his thinking said that was not expected to change.

A spokesman for Mr. Bloomberg declined to comment.

Nevertheless, Mr. Elkins’s new group points to a potential rift in the world of charter school advocacy. An organization called StudentsFirstNY has long dominated that space and continues to count Mr. Bloomberg as one of its top donors.

StudentsFirstNY successfully lobbied state lawmakers in 2023 to allow operators to open 14 charter schools by using licenses that were dormant or had been abandoned, after a four-year standstill on new charters in the city.

The group was closely aligned with former Mayor Eric Adams, paying for an ad campaign to support his bid to extend mayoral control of city schools. The group’s former leader, Jenny Sedlis, also helped raise several million dollars for a pro-Adams super PAC.

Great Public Schools New York has no such relationship with Mr. Mamdani, who remains opposed to increasing the number of charter schools.

The new group nonetheless views this as an ideal moment to push for charter school growth. New York City’s school system is losing children and is considering closing or merging hundreds of under-enrolled schools.

The charter school movement has historically been supported by wealthy donors, including Mr. Bloomberg, Daniel Loeb and Paul Singer, who oppose Mr. Mamdani on other matters like his effort to increase taxes on wealthy New Yorkers and his criticism of Israel.

The state-imposed cap on charter schools will be an immediate target for Mr. Elkins.

The first charter school law in 1998 allowed the creation of 100 charters, a ceiling that was lifted by the State Legislature to its current cap of 460 in 2010. Over the past decades, charter school enrollment statewide has grown to 190,000 students across about 355 schools, a small fraction of the state’s roughly 2.4 million public schoolchildren.

Most charter schools in the state are in New York City, where the growth has been concentrated in the Bronx and Brooklyn.

The drive for more charter schools may be aided by the continuing pressure on Mr. Mamdani to release a plan to desegregate schools. Black and Latino students make up 89 percent of charter school students.

Tresha Ward, chief executive of Prospect Schools in Brooklyn, a charter network with 3,100 students at nine schools, said that she supported the mayor’s affordability and school integration goals and that there were lessons from her schools that could be shared with the city.

The network intentionally seeks to mirror the diversity of the city and has 30 percent each of Black, Latino and white students. But because of a lack of parity in funding, the school has had trouble hiring special education teachers and cannot offer a prekindergarten program or provide free after-school care.

“I think people who voted for Mayor Mamdani and families who are choosing charters are not a divergent set of stakeholders with different interests,” Ms. Ward said. “New York is expensive. I think families are looking for a reason to stay here, and I think quality of schools is a big reason.”

Several Democratic lawmakers who supported charter schools said the landscape had changed because of efforts by StudentsFirstNY. The group’s spending strategy includes contributions to elected officials.

State Senator Kevin Parker, a Democrat, described himself as a “public school kid” who was wary of the encroachment of charter schools when he became a legislator.

“I originally had in mind the dichotomy we were being taught, that these charter schools were a threat to traditional public schools,” he said. “When I think about my support for charter schools, no longer do I think about it as a dichotomy.”

Matthew Haag contributed reporting.
